1.text: Most myths end with the hero winning.
The Norse myths tell you almost from the start exactly how everybody dies.
Odin knows a wolf will swallow him whole.
Thor knows he'll win his greatest fight and die nine steps later, and they fight anyway.
This is Ragnarök, a three-year winter, a wolf that eats the sun, a ship built from the fingernails of the dead, a battle that kills almost every god, and a fire that burns the world.
And then the part people forget, the world comes back.
Here's exactly what happens in order.

2.text: Almost everything comes from two Icelandic books from the 1200s: the Poetic Edda, especially a poem called Völuspá, where Odin raises a dead seeress and demands to know the future, and the Prose Edda by Snorri Sturluson, who retells it as a conversation.
The oldest copy of the Poetic Edda is a calfskin manuscript called the Codex Regius, written around twelve seventy.
In Völuspá, the seeress tells Odin what she sees coming, and she keeps asking him one question, like a drumbeat: do you understand yet?
Snorri was no monk. He was a powerful Icelandic chieftain and poet, and he wrote his Edda as a handbook for poets who wanted to understand the old stories.
One warning: both were written down by Christians centuries after the old religion faded, so historians debate how much of the ending is purely Norse.
I'll flag where the sources disagree.
The word Ragnarök itself means the fate of the gods, though some manuscripts say the twilight of the gods, and that small difference tells you how messy these sources are.

3.text: The death of Baldur.
Ragnarök does not begin with a battle. It begins with a funeral.
It starts with Baldur, Odin's radiant, beloved son.
After dreaming of his own death, his mother, Frigg, makes everything in the world swear never to harm him.
Fire swears, and water, and iron, and every metal. Stones swear, and trees, and diseases, and every beast, bird, and snake.
The gods turn it into a game, throwing weapons and watching them bounce off.
But Loki learns Frigg skipped one plant, mistletoe, too young to bother with.
He makes a dart from it, hands it to Baldur's blind brother, Höðr, and guides his aim.
Baldur drops dead.
And they cannot take revenge, because the place is sacred ground.
The goddess Hel will release him only if every living thing weeps.
Everything does, except one giantess in a cave.
Baldur stays dead, and many say that giantess was Loki in disguise.
Odin understands what this means. In the seeress's vision, Baldur's death is the first crack in the world.
Loki's punishment.
The gods bind Loki in a cave with the entrails of his own son and hang a venomous snake above his face.
His wife, Sigyn, catches the venom in a bowl, but when she has to empty it, the poison hits him and he thrashes.
The Norse said that was what caused earthquakes.
When Loki breaks free, it's over.
To understand why, you need to know Loki's children.
Loki fathered three monsters with a giantess: the wolf Fenrir, the world serpent Jormungandr, and Hel, who is half living and half dead.
Odin hurled the serpent into the sea, where it grew until it circled the whole earth and bit its own tail.
And the gods raised Fenrir themselves, until he grew so huge that they were afraid.
So they asked the dwarves for a ribbon called Gleipnir, made from the sound of a cat's footsteps, the beard of a woman, the roots of a mountain, and the breath of a fish.
Fenrir smelled a trick. He agreed to be tied only if one god put a hand in his mouth as a pledge. Only Týr dared.
The ribbon held. Fenrir bit down. And Týr lost his right hand, but the wolf stayed bound until the end of the world.
Fimbulwinter.
The countdown is a winter, not one, but three in a row with no summer between.
Snow blows in from every side, and the sun gives no warmth.
Human society collapses.
Brothers kill brothers.
Oaths are broken.
The seeress describes the world before the end like this: an age of axes, an age of swords, shields split in two, an age of wind, an age of wolves, before the world crashes down.
Everything that holds a society together is cut away, one thing at a time.
Then the alarm sounds.
Three roosters crow, one among the giants, one among the gods, one in the halls of the dead, and in the cave of Gnipahellir, the hound Garm howls.
It has begun.

4.text: Two wolves have chased the sun and moon since the beginning.
Now they catch them.
The sky goes dark, and the stars vanish.
Their names are Sköll and Hati. Sköll takes the sun, and Hati takes the moon.
The earth shakes so hard that mountains fall, and every chain in the world snaps.
That frees Loki, and it frees Fenrir, the monstrous wolf the gods once tricked and bound.
Fenrir charges with his lower jaw scraping the ground and his upper jaw touching the sky.
Flames burn from his eyes and nostrils.
Beside him comes his brother, Jormungandr, the world serpent, who has circled the earth in the ocean.
He heaves out of the sea, flooding the land and spitting venom across the sky.
The ship Naglfar, built from the nails of the dead, breaks loose on the flood, packed with giants, with Loki at the helm.
From the south ride the sons of Muspel, led by the fire giant Surtr, whose sword outshines the sun.
They cross Bifrost, the rainbow bridge, and it breaks beneath them.
Bifrost is the only road between heaven and earth. And now it is gone.
Heimdall, watchman of the gods, blows Gjallarhorn, and all nine worlds hear it.
Odin rides to the well of Mimir for counsel.
That well is where Odin once gave up an eye for wisdom. Now he asks it for advice one last time.
The world tree Yggdrasil shakes.
In Valhalla, Odin's hall, there are five hundred and forty doors, and eight hundred warriors can march through each one side by side.
Then the gods arm themselves, along with the warriors of Valhalla, chosen to die in battle and wait for exactly this day, and ride out to meet the end.

5.text: The armies meet on a plain called Vigridr, a hundred leagues across.
It plays out as a series of duels, each god against the enemy they were always meant to face.
The odds are not even. Gods who can die against monsters who cannot be reasoned with, and every one of them knows exactly how it ends.
Odin versus Fenrir.
Odin charges in a golden helmet with his spear Gungnir.
Fenrir swallows him whole.
The father of the gods is gone, exactly as the prophecy said.
But Odin’s silent son Vidar steps forward, wearing a thick shoe made from every scrap of leather ever trimmed from shoes.
He plants it on the wolf’s lower jaw, grips the upper, and tears Fenrir apart.
In another version, he stabs it through the heart.
Thor versus Jormungandr.
Thor meets the serpent he once fished for and nearly killed.
Their last meeting was out at sea, when Thor used an ox head as bait and hauled the whole serpent up to his boat.
This time, Mjölnir finishes it.
Thor takes nine steps away.
Then the venom catches up, and he falls dead.
Freyr versus Surtr.
Freyr faces the lord of fire without his sword because he gave it away long ago to win the giantess Gerd.
He has only an antler.
That sword could fight by itself, and without it, even a god can run out of luck.
Surtr kills him.
Týr versus Garm.
Týr, who lost his hand binding Fenrir, fights the hound of Hel.
They kill each other.
Heimdall versus Loki.
Old enemies face to face at last.
Both die.
Heimdall, who sees for a hundred miles and hears the grass grow, never saw this one coming.
Odin, Thor, Freyr, Týr, Heimdall.
Gone in moments.
The gods who held the world together are gone, and what is left will burn.
The prophecy was exact.

6.text: When the last god has fallen, Surtr is still standing.
He hurls fire across the world.
The stars fall, and the earth sinks beneath the sea.
That's the end of the world, but not the end of the story.
The seeress looks once more and sees the earth rising from the sea, green and fresh, with fields growing crops no one planted.
Waterfalls tumble from the new hills, and an eagle flies over them, hunting fish.
A few gods survive: Vidar and Vali, sons of Odin, and Modi and Magni, sons of Thor, who inherit Mjollnir.
They meet on the old field of Idavellir and find the golden game pieces the gods once played with.
Then, Baldur and Hodur return from the dead, reconciled.
The sun had a daughter before the wolf swallowed her, just as bright, and she takes her mother's place.
Two humans, Lif and Lifthrasir, hid through the fire and now repopulate the world.
They survived by hiding in a wood called Hoddmimir's Holt, living on the morning dew.
And the seeress glimpses a hall roofed in gold called Gimle, where the righteous live.
In that hall, the seeress says, there is joy forever.
The dragon Nidhogg still flies by, carrying corpses on his wings.
Then the seeress sinks back down, and the vision ends.

7.text: In almost every other mythology, the gods can't lose.
In the Norse world, they can, and they know it.
Odin spent his whole life collecting knowledge to escape this fate. He hung from a tree, gave up an eye, and still could not change it.
The whole point is what they do with that knowledge.
They prepare and they ride out.
For the Vikings, courage meant standing your ground when you know how it ends.
There is a famous line in the Havamal: cattle die, kinsmen die, you yourself will die, but fame never dies for the one who earns a good name.
And the world burns and the world returns.
Nothing is permanent, not even the end.
Some scholars think the rebirth was shaped by Christian ideas, and some think it is much older. Nobody can prove it.
